passage: A month after the auto-rickshaw he was riding in skidded into a divider, Irfan still woke at 3 a.m. with his heart racing. Every horn on the road outside made his shoulders jump. He kept his morning routine anyway: tea, a short walk, the office bus at 8:40. At lunch his colleague Pooja noticed he had barely touched his rice. "You keep flinching," she said quietly. "It's been weeks. I should be over it," Irfan muttered. "I didn't tell the driver to slow down. Maybe if I had..." Pooja shook her head. "You were a passenger." She pulled up the number of the hospital's counselling desk on her phone. He looked at it for a long moment, then typed it into his own.

qa.q: How long after the crash did Irfan still wake at 3 a.m. with his heart racing?
qa.a: A month after the auto-rickshaw skidded into a divider, he still woke at 3 a.m. with his heart racing.

qa.q: Why does Irfan say he should be over it?
qa.a: He seems to think he is failing at recovering and blames himself, wondering whether telling the driver to slow down might have changed things.

qa.q: What would you advise Irfan to do next?
qa.a: Keep his daily routine going and actually call the hospital's counselling desk, since trained help suits a body that stays on alert after a scare.

qa.q: How does Pooja see Irfan's situation?
qa.a: She sees a colleague who is flinching and not eating, and who is not to blame because he was only a passenger, so she offers a concrete way to get help.

grounding: After a frightening accident the body stays alert and sleep is disturbed; Irfan keeps routines, is told it was not his fault, and takes down a counselling number.

passage:
Three weeks after the car crash on the Pacific Highway, Daniel still couldn't sleep past 3 a.m. Every time a truck braked outside his Sydney flat, his heart slammed and his hands went slick. He'd stopped driving. He took two buses to work instead.

He told himself he should be over it. Nobody had died. He'd walked away with bruises.

At lunch, his colleague Chen noticed him flinch at a dropped tray. "You okay, mate?"

Daniel laughed it off, then didn't. "I keep reliving it. I should've braked faster. I froze."

Chen put down his sandwich. "My sister was in a crash. She said the doctor told her this is really common after something scary. Your body's still on alert. It's not weakness."

That evening Daniel booked an appointment with his GP, who referred him to a psychologist. He also started walking every morning at the same time, and cooking dinner even when he wasn't hungry. It didn't fix everything. But the nights got a little shorter.

qa.q: How long after the crash was it when Daniel still couldn't sleep past 3 a.m.?
qa.a: Three weeks after the car crash.

qa.q: What was Daniel feeling when he said "I should've braked faster"?
qa.a: He felt frightened and ashamed, blaming himself for freezing during the crash.

qa.q: What steps did Daniel take, and why were they helpful?
qa.a: Seeing his GP, getting a referral to a psychologist, and keeping routines like morning walks and cooking, which brought trained help and steadiness.

qa.q: How does Chen see Daniel's reactions?
qa.a: Chen sees them as a common response to something scary, the body still on alert, not weakness.

grounding: The passage shows someone whose body stays on alert after a frightening accident, learning these reactions are common, seeking trained help, keeping routines and easing self-blame.

passage:
Two weeks after a patient's relative attacked staff in the emergency ward at the Kottayam hospital, Rukmini was back on night shift. She hadn't been hurt badly, only a bruised arm. But every time the doors slammed, her whole body went rigid. She'd stopped sleeping more than a few hours.

On her break, she sat in the staff room with Jomon, who had been on shift that night too.

"I keep thinking I should have stepped in faster," she said. "Or called security earlier."

"You got the child out of the way," Jomon said. "I saw you. You did what you could in seconds."

She stared at her tea. "Then why can't I stop shaking?"

"Because it was frightening. My hands still shake too." He pulled a leaflet from his pocket. "The hospital's arranging counselling for everyone on that shift. Thursday. I'm going. Come with me?"

She took the leaflet. On Thursday, they went together. She kept her morning walk and her sister's Sunday calls too. It helped, a little at a time.

qa.q: What did Jomon say Rukmini did during the attack?
qa.a: She got the child out of the way.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling on her break?
qa.a: She felt frightened and guilty, shaking and blaming herself for not stepping in faster.

qa.q: What helped Rukmini begin to recover?
qa.a: Going to the hospital's counselling with Jomon, keeping her routines, and hearing from him that her reactions were normal.

qa.q: How does Jomon see Rukmini's actions that night?
qa.a: Jomon sees that she did what she could in seconds and protected a child, and admits he is still shaken too.

grounding: The passage shows someone whose body stays on alert and sleep is disturbed after violence at work, seeking trained help, keeping routines and learning not to blame herself.
